Mridul sent me the page for that "guaranteed placement" course at breakfast. "Didi, look, 4.9 stars!"
I looked. Four hundred reviews, and every single one says something like "Best decision of my life, got job in 3 months." Nobody complains about anything. Not the timings, not the videos, not the fees. Real people complain about something. That made me uneasy.
I sorted by date: sixty reviews on one day in March. Then I clicked the three-star filter. Zero. Zero three-star reviews out of four hundred?
On a student forum I found a long thread from people who had actually done it. Mixed. Some liked the mentors. Several said the "placement" was a list of job links.
I sent Mridul the thread instead of a lecture. He replied, "ok will ask sir at college before paying anything."
Relieved. Also a bit proud of myself.
Irawati

At about eleven, Kamal rushed over with his phone. "Child-lifting gang in our area! Strangers in a white van. Forward to everyone!" The message had a blurry photo, lots of red text, and "SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS".

Jahnavi, you asked why I never forward anything on the office group. Let me tell you about my first job, at a small newspaper in Madurai, when I was twenty-four.
One evening a typed letter came in: the town's cooperative bank was about to collapse, and everyone should take their money out by Friday. My colleague Selvam wanted it on the front page. "People have a right to know!"
It frightened me too. My own mother's savings were in that bank. But I asked: who sent this, and who gains if half the town rushes to the counter tomorrow? There was no name, only a post-box number.
I held it back until morning and phoned the bank's auditor. The accounts were fine. The post box belonged to a man in a court case with the bank.
"Keerthana, you're a coward," Selvam said, every day for a week. Nothing was printed. Nothing happened. That quiet nothing is what I'm proudest of.

Okay, this is Pankaj, and for the school podcast I want to talk about the fake notice.
In March a notice went round saying our school was closed because of a gas leak. It had the logo, the principal's signature, everything. Half the class stayed home. I watched my neighbour Ritwik forward it to eleven groups. He wasn't lying on purpose. He genuinely looked scared for his little sister.
Later our friend Gautam found out who made it: a boy from another school who runs a meme page. He did it for followers. His page grew by thousands that day.
Gautam put it simply. Some people make fakes for money, some for clicks, some for power, some just to be cruel. And the people who share them usually believe them.
That changed something for me. Now when I see a shocking notice, I don't panic, and I don't blame the forwarder. I ask: who gains from this? Then I check the school's own page.

qa.a: Asking who gains from the message, then checking the school's own page before reacting or forwarding.

qa.a: Ritwik looked genuinely scared for his little sister, so the notice felt true to him even though it was fake.

Everyone calls me Chinmay the backbencher, and from the back I saw Joseph's face when the screenshot came up. It showed a chat, supposedly from our maths teacher, mocking the weak students by name. Joseph's name was on it. He went red and forwarded it to the class group with "see what she really thinks of us".
By second period everyone had it. Mrs Thomas, our class teacher, walked in, put her phone on the desk and said, "Let's talk about this."
She showed us that the chat bubbles used the wrong font and the time said 25:10. Then she asked why someone would make it. Hands went up. "For fun." "For likes." "To get her in trouble." She nodded. "And why did people share it?"
Nobody answered. I looked at Joseph. He was staring at his desk. I'm not sure what he felt. I felt a bit sick, because I'd believed it too, and it was easier to believe about a teacher I didn't like.

qa.a: Joseph's own name was on it, so it hurt and felt true to him, and he shared it before checking.

The message reached Tariq at 11 pm in his student flat in Lyon: a still from a video that showed his face on someone else's body, doing something he had never done. "Pay 500 euros by morning or your family and your university get this."
His hands went cold. He read it four times. His first thought was to pay, just to make it stop.
Diego, his flatmate, found him sitting on the kitchen floor. Tariq turned the screen around without a word.
"That's not you," Diego said. "Look at the neck. And even if it looked perfect, this is on them, not you."
They didn't reply to the sender. Diego helped him screenshot everything: the account name, the messages, the time. They reported the account on the app and filled in the police's online cybercrime form that night. Then Tariq called his uncle in Marseille, voice shaking. "I'm glad you told me," his uncle said. "We'll go to the police station together in the morning."

qa.a: Tariq felt cold panic and shame, reading it four times and wanting to pay just to make it stop.

qa.a: They did not reply, saved screenshots of the account, messages and time, reported the account on the app, filed the police cybercrime form, and Tariq told his uncle.

qa.a: Diego saw at once that the image was fake and that the blame belonged to the sender, not Tariq, which helped Tariq stop freezing.

I'm Zubin. When we moved to Pune in Class 10, I didn't know a single person. Lunch was the worst part.
Then some older students invited me to "the Circle". Music, long talks on a terrace, everyone hugging when you arrive. Within a week they knew my birthday and my favourite song. It felt amazing to be wanted.

I went into the kitchen and told Mum everything. She put her tea down, listened without interrupting, and said, "Wanting friends is not wrong. Asking you to keep secrets from us is." She called the school counsellor right then and set up a meeting for the next day.

Class teacher's note, Class 9B, Thursday
For three weeks Jeevan, who used to sit alone at lunch, has been glowing. He talks about his "crew" from an online group: daily 5 am check-ins, a special greeting, older members who call him "brother". I was glad at first. He needed friends.
This week things changed. He stopped sitting with Lokesh, his one friend in class. Lokesh told me Jeevan said the crew wants him to "cut off anyone who doesn't get it". Today, when I asked where the crew meets in person, Jeevan would only say it was "secret for now".

He looked relieved, and a bit scared. With him beside me, I called his mother the same afternoon and informed the school counsellor, who will see him tomorrow.
